title: git
description: Git is a free, open-source distributed version control system created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage Linux kernel development.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
This page covers installing Git and the handful of settings you need
before your first commit.

## 1. Install Git

| Platform | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Arch Linux | `sudo pacman -S git` |
| Debian / Ubuntu | `sudo apt install git` |
| Fedora | `sudo dnf install git` |
| openSUSE | `sudo zypper install git` |
| macOS (Homebrew) | `brew install git` |
| macOS (Xcode CLT) | `xcode-select --install` |
| Windows | Install [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win), which bundles Git Bash |

Verify it installed correctly:

```bash
git --version
```

## 2. Set your identity

Every commit records an author name and email. Set these once, globally,
and every repository on the machine will use them unless overridden:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

To use different identity per project (common if you separate work and
personal commits), drop `--global` and run the same commands from inside
that repository — the setting is written to `.git/config` instead of
`~/.gitconfig`.

## 3. Pick a default editor

Git opens an editor for commit messages, interactive rebases, and merge
conflicts when you don’t pass `-m`. The default is usually `vi`; change
it if you’d rather use something else:

```bash
git config --global core.editor "nano"        # or "code --wait", "vim", etc.
```

## 4. Set the default branch name (optional)

Since Git 2.28, the initial branch name on `git init` is configurable. Most
hosts (GitHub, GitLab) default new repositories to `main`:

```bash
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

## 5. Create or clone your first repository

Starting a brand-new project:

```bash
mkdir my-project && cd my-project
git init
```

Or grab an existing one:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/git/git.git
```

Continue to [Basic Workflow](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/basic-workflow/) for the everyday
add/commit/push loop, or [How Git Works](/git/0.0.0/how-git-works/objects-&-the-.git-directory/) if you’d
like to understand what `git init` actually created before touching
anything else. Once the basics feel familiar, [Learn by
Examples](/git/0.0.0/learn-by-examples/starting-the-project/) walks through a
whole real project — branching, conflicts, mistakes, releases, and
collaboration — as one continuous story.

## 6. Authenticating with a remote host

Pushing to GitHub, GitLab, or similar over HTTPS now requires a
**personal access token** instead of your account password — generate
one from the host’s settings and use it in place of a password when
prompted. Over SSH, generate a key pair and add the public key to your
account instead:

```
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub    # paste this into your host's SSH keys settings
```

See [Configuration](/git/0.0.0/reference/configuration/) for credential helpers that
avoid re-entering a token on every push.

## Shell completion & a few global settings worth setting once

Bash and Zsh completion scripts ship with Git itself (or your distro's
`git` package). Arch Linux installs completion automatically; on
other systems you may need to source it manually:

```
# bash, if not already sourced by your distro
source /usr/share/bash-completion/completions/git

# zsh (works out of the box if you use oh-my-zsh's git plugin)
autoload -Uz compinit && compinit
```

A handful of global settings pay for themselves within the first week:

```bash
git config --global pull.rebase false     # or true/merges — pick one deliberately, see FAQ
git config --global core.editor "nvim"    # or vim, code --wait, etc.
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global color.ui auto
git config --global help.autocorrect 10   # auto-run close typo matches after a short delay
```
Getting Started.A Complete Walkthrough:
The other pages in these docs are organized by topic. This one is organized by **time** — one continuous, realistic story, with the actual folder contents and file contents shown at every step, so you can see *why* each command matters instead of memorizing it in isolation. We’ll build a tiny project, branch it, break it, fix it, and push it. ## 1. An empty folder is not a repository Before `git init`, a folder is just a folder — Git knows nothing about it: ``` $ mkdir hello-git && cd hello-git $ ls -la total 0 drwxr-xr-x 2 psdk psdk 40 Aug 27 10:00 . drwxr-xr-x 30 psdk psdk 960 Aug 27 10:00 .. ``` ``` $ git init Initialized empty Git repository in /home/psdk/hello-git/.git/ ``` Now look at the folder again: ``` hello-git/ └── .git/ ← the entire repository lives in here ├── HEAD ├── config ├── objects/ ├── refs/ └── ... ``` Nothing about your actual files changed — there aren’t any yet. All `git init` did was create `.git/`, an (initially almost empty) database that will track every version of every file you ever add. See [Objects & the .git Directory](/git/0.0.0/how-git-works/objects-&-the-.git-directory/) for exactly what lives in there. ``` $ git status On branch main No commits yet nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track) ``` ## 2. Adding your first file Create a real file: ``` $ cat > index.html << 'EOF' Hello Git

Hello, Git!

EOF ``` The folder now has one real file next to the hidden repository: ``` hello-git/ ├── .git/ └── index.html ``` Git notices it, but isn’t tracking it yet — that’s the difference between **untracked** and **staged**: ``` $ git status On branch main No commits yet Untracked files: (use "git add ..." to include in what will be committed) index.html nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track) ``` ``` $ git add index.html $ git status On branch main No commits yet Changes to be committed: (use "git rm --cached ..." to unstage) new file: index.html ``` ``` $ git commit -m "Add homepage" [main (root-commit) 3af92c1] Add homepage 1 file changed, 6 insertions(+) create mode 100644 index.html ``` `3af92c1` is the new commit’s SHA — a fingerprint of its content, parent, author, and message. Nothing about the folder on disk changed (`index.html` is still just sitting there); what changed is that `.git/` now has a permanent, addressable snapshot of it. See [Basic Workflow](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/basic-workflow/) for the full add/commit toolkit. ## 3. Editing the file and seeing exactly what changed ``` $ sed -i 's/Hello, Git!/Hello, World!/' index.html $ git diff diff --git a/index.html b/index.html index 3af92c1..91bce02 100644 --- a/index.html +++ b/index.html @@ -3,5 +3,5 @@ Hello Git -

Hello, Git!

+

Hello, World!

``` Git didn’t store "the file changed" as a vague event — `git diff` computed this line-by-line comparison on the fly, between what’s on disk right now and the last thing you committed. Commit it: ``` $ git commit -am "Change heading text" [main 91bce02] Change heading text 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-) ``` ## 4. Branching off to try something risky You want to add a stylesheet, but you’re not sure it’ll work out. A branch lets you try it without touching `main` at all: ``` $ git switch -c feature/add-styles Switched to a new branch 'feature/add-styles' $ cat > style.css << 'EOF' h1 { color: teal; font-family: sans-serif; } EOF $ git add style.css $ git commit -m "Add stylesheet" [feature/add-styles 5c1e0aa] Add stylesheet 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) create mode 100644 style.css ``` On this branch, the folder now has three files: ``` hello-git/ (branch: feature/add-styles) ├── .git/ ├── index.html └── style.css ← only exists on this branch, so far ``` Now switch back: ``` $ git switch main Switched to branch 'main' $ ls index.html ``` `style.css` is gone from the folder — not deleted, just not part of what `main` points to. Git rewrote the working directory to match `main`’s snapshot exactly. Switch back to `feature/add-styles` and it reappears instantly, because it was never actually erased, only swapped out. This is the entire trick behind branches being "cheap": see [Objects & the .git Directory](/git/0.0.0/how-git-works/objects-&-the-.git-directory/) for why. ## 5. Merging the branch back in Before merging, the two branches point at different commits, both sharing the same history up to the point they diverged: ```yaml main: A---B \ feature/add-styles: C ``` ``` $ git switch main $ git merge feature/add-styles Updating 91bce02..5c1e0aa Fast-forward style.css | 1 + 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) ``` `main` hadn’t moved since the branch was created, so Git could just slide the `main` pointer forward to `C` — no new commit needed: ``` main, feature/add-styles: A---B---C ``` See [Branching & Merging](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/branching-&-merging/) for what happens instead when the branches *have* diverged (a real three-way merge commit with two parents). ## 6. Causing (and resolving) a real conflict Conflicts happen when two branches edit the **same lines** differently. Let’s make one on purpose: ``` $ git switch -c feature/rename-heading $ sed -i 's/Hello, World!/Welcome!/' index.html $ git commit -am "Rename heading to Welcome" $ git switch main $ sed -i 's/Hello, World!/Hi there!/' index.html $ git commit -am "Rename heading to Hi there" $ git merge feature/rename-heading Auto-merging index.html CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in index.html Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result. ``` Open `index.html` and Git has marked exactly where the two versions disagree: ```html <<<<<<< HEAD

Hi there!

=======

Welcome!

>>>>>>> feature/rename-heading ``` Everything above `=======` is your current branch (`HEAD`, i.e. `main`); everything below is the branch being merged in. Pick one, blend them, or write something new — then remove the markers entirely: ```html

Welcome to Git!

``` ```bash $ git add index.html $ git commit -m "Merge feature/rename-heading, resolve heading conflict" ``` This time Git creates a real merge commit with **two parents**, because history had genuinely diverged and needed reconciling, not just fast-forwarding: ```yaml main: A---B---C-------------M \ / feature/rename-heading: D---------● ``` See [Branching & Merging](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/branching-&-merging/) for the full conflict toolkit (`--abort`, `--ours`/`--theirs`, etc). ## 7. Connecting to a remote and pushing So far everything has lived only on this one machine. A remote is another full copy of the repository — usually on GitHub or GitLab — that you explicitly sync with: ``` $ git remote add origin git@github.com:psdk/hello-git.git $ git push -u origin main Enumerating objects: 12, done. Writing objects: 100% (12/12), 1.04 KiB | 1.04 MiB/s, done. To github.com:psdk/hello-git.git * [new branch] main -> main branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'. ``` Both copies now share the same commit history, connected by name: ``` your machine GitHub ("origin") ┌────────────────┒ ┌─────────────────┒ │ main ▪ A-B-C-M │ --push--> │ main ▪ A-B-C-M │ │ origin/main (tracks GitHub) │ <--fetch-- │ │ └─────────────────┚ └─────────────────┚ ``` See [Remotes](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/remotes/) for fetch vs. pull, tracking branches, and working with forks. ## 8. Undoing a real mistake Say you accidentally committed a secrets file: ``` $ echo "API_KEY=super-secret-value" > .env $ git add .env $ git commit -m "oops, added env file" [main 7d4a1f0] oops, added env file 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+) create mode 100644 .env ``` It hasn’t been pushed yet, so it's safe to undo completely: ``` $ git reset --hard HEAD~1 HEAD is now at ... Merge feature/rename-heading, resolve heading conflict $ ls -la .git/ index.html style.css ← .env is gone, and so is that commit ``` Add it to `.gitignore` so it can’t happen again: ```bash $ echo ".env" > .gitignore $ git add .gitignore $ git commit -m "Ignore .env files" ``` If the bad commit had *already* been pushed and pulled by someone else, `reset --hard` would be the wrong tool — you'd want `git revert` instead, which undoes the change with a new commit rather than rewriting shared history. The full decision guide is in [Undoing Changes](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/undoing-changes/). ## Where to go from here | You just saw… | Go deeper | | --- | --- | | What .git/ actually contains | [Objects & the .git Directory](/git/0.0.0/how-git-works/objects-&-the-.git-directory/) | | add / commit / diff / log | [Basic Workflow](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/basic-workflow/) | | Branching, fast-forward vs. real merges, conflicts | [Branching & Merging](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/branching-&-merging/) | | reset --hard, and safer alternatives | [Undoing Changes](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/undoing-changes/) | | push, fetch vs. pull, remotes | [Remotes](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/remotes/) |

How Git Works.Objects & the .git Directory:
Most Git confusion disappears once you understand what’s actually stored
on disk. Git is, underneath the porcelain commands, a simple
**content-addressed key-value store** built on four object types.

## The .git directory

`git init` creates a `.git/` directory that *is* the repository — delete
it and the version history is gone, even though your files remain. Its most
important pieces:

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `.git/objects/` | Every blob, tree, commit, and tag, stored compressed by content hash |
| `.git/refs/heads/` | One file per local branch, containing the commit SHA it points to |
| `.git/refs/tags/` | One file per tag |
| `.git/refs/remotes/` | Remote-tracking branches, e.g. `origin/main` |
| `.git/HEAD` | A pointer to the currently checked-out ref (usually `refs/heads/<branch>`) |
| `.git/index` | The staging area — a binary file listing what will go into the next commit |
| `.git/config` | Repository-local configuration |
| `.git/logs/` | The reflog: a history of where `HEAD` and branches have pointed |

## The four object types

Everything Git tracks is one of these, each identified by the SHA of its
own contents:

- **Blob** — the raw contents of a single file. No filename, no
  metadata, just bytes. Two files with identical content share one blob.
- **Tree** — a directory listing: a set of (mode, name, SHA) entries
  pointing at blobs and other trees. This is where filenames live.
- **Commit** — a snapshot pointer: one tree SHA (the project root at
  that moment), zero or more parent commit SHAs, author, committer,
  timestamp, and message.
- **Tag** — (for annotated tags) a named, signable pointer at a
  specific commit, with its own message and metadata.

You can inspect any of these directly:

```bash
git cat-file -t <sha>      # print the object type
git cat-file -p <sha>      # print the object contents
git log --oneline -1       # find a commit SHA to try this on
```

## Refs and HEAD

A **ref** is just a named pointer to a commit SHA, stored as a small file
under `.git/refs/`. A **branch** is nothing more than a ref that moves
forward automatically every time you commit while it’s checked out — which
is why creating a branch is instantaneous and cheap: Git writes one 40 (or
64) character line to a file, it doesn’t copy any content.

`HEAD` is a pointer to the ref you currently have checked out. Most of the
time it points at a branch (`ref: refs/heads/main`), which in turn points
at a commit. When you check out a specific commit or tag instead of a
branch, `HEAD` points directly at that commit — a state called
**detached HEAD**.

## The three trees

Day-to-day Git commands move changes between three areas:

| Area | What it is | Command to move in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Working directory | The actual files on disk you edit | — |
| Staging area / index | A snapshot of what will go into the *next* commit | `git add` |
| Repository (`.git/objects`) | Permanent, committed history | `git commit` |

This intermediate staging step is what lets you build a commit out of only
part of your working-directory changes — run `git add -p` to stage
individual hunks instead of whole files.

## What git commit actually does

1. Reads the current staging area (the index).
2. Writes a blob for every changed file’s contents (skipped if that exact
   content already exists as a blob).
3. Writes tree objects representing the full directory structure of what’s
   staged.
4. Writes a commit object pointing at the root tree and at the current
   commit as its parent.
5. Moves the current branch ref to point at the new commit.

Because every commit stores the state of the *entire* project tree (not a
diff), Git can check out any commit directly without replaying history —
diffs you see in `git log -p` or `git diff` are computed on the fly by
comparing two trees.

> Once you have this mental model, the "everyday" commands stop feeling
> like memorized incantations: `git branch foo` writes a ref file,
> `git checkout foo` moves `HEAD`, `git merge` creates a new commit with two
> parents, and `git reset` just moves a ref (and optionally the index and
> working directory) to point somewhere else.

## Packfiles & garbage collection

Loose objects (one file per object, as described above) are simple but
wasteful — Git periodically compacts them into **packfiles**, which
store many objects together with delta compression against similar objects.
This is what makes cloning a large repository’s history reasonably small
on disk and over the network.

```bash
git gc                 # pack loose objects, prune unreachable ones after a grace period
git gc --aggressive    # spend more time for better delta compression (rarely needed)
git count-objects -v   # see how many loose objects/packs you currently have
```

Git runs a lightweight `gc` automatically after commands like
`commit` and `fetch` once enough loose objects accumulate, so you
rarely need to run it by hand. Objects become **unreachable** (eligible
for pruning) when nothing — no branch, tag, or reflog entry — points to them
anymore, which is why a `reset --hard` from earlier is still
recoverable via `reflog` for a while: the commit object hasn’t
actually been deleted yet.

## A worked example: what one commit actually contains

Take a tiny repo with two files:

```
hello-git/
├── index.html
└── style.css
```

After `git add .` and `git commit -m "Initial commit"`, four
objects exist in `.git/objects/` — one commit, one tree, and one
blob per file:

```
$ git cat-file -p HEAD
tree 8f2e1a9c4b7d3e6f1a0c9b8d7e6f5a4b3c2d1e0f
author psdk <you@example.com> 1735000000 +0000
committer psdk <you@example.com> 1735000000 +0000

Initial commit

$ git cat-file -p 8f2e1a9c4b7d3e6f1a0c9b8d7e6f5a4b3c2d1e0f
100644 blob 3af92c1d8e5b2f4a6c1d0e9b8a7c6d5e4f3a2b1c    index.html
100644 blob 91bce02f3a6d5c4b2e1f0a9b8c7d6e5f4a3b2c1d    style.css

$ git cat-file -p 3af92c1d8e5b2f4a6c1d0e9b8a7c6d5e4f3a2b1c
<!doctype html>
<html>...
```

Visually, that's a small tree of pointers, all the way down to actual
file bytes:

```
commit "Initial commit"
  └── tree (the root folder snapshot)
        ├── blob "index.html"'s content
        └── blob "style.css"'s content
```

Edit only `index.html` and commit again, and the second commit's
tree reuses the *exact same* `style.css` blob — unchanged
content always hashes to the same SHA, so Git doesn't store it twice. Only
a new blob (the edited file), a new tree (pointing at the new blob and the
same old one), and a new commit get created.

Everyday Git.Basic Workflow:
This is the loop you’ll run dozens of times a day: check what changed,
stage it, commit it, inspect history.

## Starting a repository

```bash
git init                                   # new, empty repository here
git clone <url>                            # copy an existing repository
git clone <url> my-dir                     # ...into a specific directory
git clone --depth 1 <url>                  # shallow clone: history from HEAD only
```

## git status

The single most-run Git command. Shows the current branch, files staged
for commit, files modified but not staged, and untracked files:

```bash
git status
git status -s      # short format: one line per file
```

Short-format prefixes: `M` modified, `A` added, `D` deleted, `R` renamed,
`??` untracked, and a staged change shows in the first column vs. an
unstaged one in the second (e.g. `M  file` is staged, `M file` is not).

## Staging changes

```bash
git add file.txt              # stage one file
git add dir/                  # stage a directory
git add .                     # stage everything in and below the cwd
git add -A                    # stage everything in the whole repo
git add -p                    # interactively stage hunks within files
```

## Committing

```bash
git commit -m "Short summary of the change"
git commit                    # opens $EDITOR for a longer message
git commit -am "message"      # stage every tracked, modified file, then commit
git commit --amend            # rewrite the most recent commit
```

A well-formed commit message is a short (~50 char) summary line, a blank
line, then optional detail wrapped at ~72 characters explaining *why*, not
just *what*.

> `--amend` rewrites history — only use it on commits you haven’t pushed
> yet, or that you’re certain nobody else has already pulled.

## Inspecting changes

```bash
git diff                      # working directory vs. staging area
git diff --staged             # staging area vs. last commit (a.k.a. --cached)
git diff HEAD                 # working directory vs. last commit
git diff main..feature        # compare two branches
git diff -- path/to/file       # limit to one path
```

## Viewing history

```bash
git log                                   # full history, newest first
git log --oneline                         # one line per commit
git log --oneline --graph --all           # ASCII graph of every branch
git log -p                                # show the diff for each commit
git log -n 5                              # last 5 commits
git log --author="Name"                   # filter by author
git log --since="2 weeks ago"             # filter by date
git log -- path/to/file                   # history of one file
git show <sha>                            # full details of one commit
```

## Removing and renaming

```bash
git rm file.txt                # delete a file and stage the deletion
git rm --cached file.txt       # stop tracking a file, keep it on disk
git mv old.txt new.txt         # rename/move, staged automatically
```

## Ignoring files

Create a `.gitignore` file listing patterns Git should never track or
prompt you about — build output, dependencies, secrets:

```
# .gitignore
.env
node_modules/
build/
*.log
.dart_tool/
```

Already-tracked files aren’t affected retroactively by `.gitignore`; untrack
them first with `git rm --cached`.

Next: [Branching & Merging](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/branching-&-merging/) to work on
more than one line of development at once.

## A few flags worth memorizing early

| Command | Why it’s useful |
| --- | --- |
| `git add -p` | Review and stage changes hunk-by-hunk instead of whole files |
| `git commit --amend` | Fix the message or add forgotten changes to the last commit (before pushing) |
| `git log -p -- path/to/file` | Show the full diff history of a single file |
| `git log --stat` | Show which files changed and by how many lines, per commit |
| `git diff --word-diff` | Highlight changed words instead of whole lines — great for prose |
| `git blame -L 10,20 file` | See who last touched each line in a specific range |

A common early mistake is committing far too much in one go. Small,
focused commits with a clear message make `log`, `blame`, and
`bisect` (see [Bisecting](/git/0.0.0/advanced/bisecting/)) dramatically more
useful later — think of each commit as a checkpoint you might want to
return to individually.
Everyday Git.Branching & Merging:
A branch is a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit (see
[How Git Works](/git/0.0.0/how-git-works/objects-&-the-.git-directory/)). Branching lets you develop
features, fixes, and experiments in isolation without disturbing `main`.

## Creating and switching branches

```bash
git branch                       # list local branches
git branch -a                    # list local + remote-tracking branches
git branch feature-x              # create a branch (doesn't switch to it)
git switch feature-x              # switch to it
git switch -c feature-x           # create + switch in one step
git checkout feature-x            # older equivalent of switch
git checkout -b feature-x         # older equivalent of switch -c
```

`switch` and `restore` (Git 2.23+) split `checkout`’s overloaded
responsibilities — changing branches vs. discarding file changes — into
two clearer commands. Both still work; newer tutorials favor `switch`.

## Renaming and deleting branches

```bash
git branch -m old-name new-name    # rename
git branch -d feature-x            # delete (fails if unmerged)
git branch -D feature-x            # force delete
```

## Merging

Merge a branch into whichever branch you currently have checked out:

```bash
git switch main
git merge feature-x
```

Git performs one of two kinds of merge depending on history:

- **Fast-forward** — if `main` hasn’t moved since `feature-x` branched
  off, Git just moves the `main` pointer forward to `feature-x`’s tip. No
  new commit is created. Force a real merge commit anyway with
  `git merge --no-ff feature-x` to keep an explicit record that a feature
  branch existed.
- **Three-way merge** — if both branches have diverged, Git compares
  the two tips against their common ancestor and creates a new
  **merge commit** with two parents, combining both histories.

## Resolving conflicts

A conflict happens when the same region of a file was changed differently
on both branches. Git pauses the merge and marks the file:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version of the line
=======
their version of the line
>>>>>>> feature-x
```

1. Open each conflicted file and edit it down to the content you want,
   removing the `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>` markers.
2. `git add` the resolved file(s).
3. `git commit` to finish the merge (Git pre-fills a merge commit
   message).

Useful commands while resolving:

```bash
git status                    # lists conflicted files
git diff                      # shows conflict markers in context
git merge --abort             # bail out and return to pre-merge state
git checkout --ours <file>    # take your side entirely for one file
git checkout --theirs <file>  # take their side entirely for one file
```

## Choosing a branching strategy

| Model | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Trunk-based | Everyone commits small changes to `main` frequently, guarded by feature flags and CI |
| GitHub Flow | Short-lived feature branches → pull request → merge to `main` → deploy |
| Git Flow | Long-lived `develop` and `main`, plus `feature/`, `release/`, and `hotfix/` branches |

Most modern teams use trunk-based development or GitHub Flow; Git Flow’s
extra ceremony is mostly reserved for projects that ship multiple
long-supported release versions in parallel.

See also: [Rebasing & Cherry-Picking](/git/0.0.0/advanced/rebasing-&-cherry-picking/)
for an alternative to merge commits that keeps history linear.

## Naming conventions & cleaning up

Consistent branch names make it obvious what a branch is for and let
tooling (CI, hooks) key off the prefix:

```
feature/checkout-redesign
fix/null-pointer-on-logout
chore/upgrade-dependencies
release/2.4.0
```

Once a branch is merged, delete it — keeping stale branches around
makes `git branch` and `git switch`’s autocomplete noisy and
easy to accidentally build on top of.

```bash
git branch --merged main            # list branches already merged into main
git branch -d $(git branch --merged main | grep -v "main")  # delete them (careful!)
git fetch --prune                   # remove local refs to remote branches that no longer exist
```

## A worked example: a real conflict, start to finish

Say `notes.md` currently contains:

```
# Project Notes

Status: in progress
```

On `main`, someone updates the status:

```bash
$ sed -i 's/in progress/blocked on design review/' notes.md
$ git commit -am "Update status: blocked"
```

Meanwhile, on a branch called `docs-fix` (created before that
commit), someone else edited the *same line* for a typo fix:

```bash
$ sed -i 's/in progress/In Progress/' notes.md
$ git commit -am "Fix capitalization"
```

Merging `docs-fix` into `main` now fails automatically, because
Git can't tell which edit to the same line should win:

```
$ git switch main
$ git merge docs-fix
Auto-merging notes.md
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in notes.md
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

`notes.md` on disk right now looks like this:

```
# Project Notes

<<<<<<< HEAD
Status: blocked on design review
=======
Status: In Progress
>>>>>>> docs-fix
```

Both edits were valid, so combine them by hand and delete the markers:

```
# Project Notes

Status: Blocked on design review
```

```bash
$ git add notes.md
$ git commit -m "Merge docs-fix, resolve status wording"
```

The resulting commit graph has a real merge commit with two parents,
since both branches' work needed reconciling rather than one simply
sliding forward onto the other:

```yaml
main:        A---B(status: blocked)-------M(merge)
                  \                      /
docs-fix:          C(capitalization)-----●
```
Everyday Git.Remotes:
A **remote** is just a named URL pointing at another copy of the
repository — typically hosted on GitHub, GitLab, or a private server.
`git clone` automatically creates a remote named `origin` pointing at the
URL you cloned from.

## Managing remotes

```bash
git remote -v                                 # list remotes and their URLs
git remote add origin git@github.com:you/repo.git
git remote rename origin upstream
git remote remove upstream
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:you/repo.git
```

## fetch vs. pull

- **`git fetch`** downloads new commits and updates
  remote-tracking branches (e.g. `origin/main`) — it never touches your
  working directory or local branches. Safe to run anytime.
- **`git pull`** is `git fetch` immediately followed by
  `git merge` (or `rebase`, with `--rebase`) into your current branch. It
  changes your working directory.

```bash
git fetch origin
git fetch --all               # fetch every remote
git pull                      # fetch + merge current branch's upstream
git pull --rebase             # fetch + rebase instead of merge
```

## Pushing

```bash
git push origin main                    # push local main to origin's main
git push -u origin main                 # also set main to track origin/main
git push                                # once tracking is set, just this works
git push origin --delete feature-x      # delete a remote branch
git push --force-with-lease             # safer force-push after rewriting history
```

> Prefer `--force-with-lease` over plain `--force`: it refuses to overwrite
> the remote branch if someone else pushed to it since your last fetch,
> whereas `--force` overwrites unconditionally.

## Tracking branches

A local branch can be linked to a remote branch so plain `git pull`/
`git push` know where to sync:

```bash
git branch -u origin/main          # set upstream for the current branch
git branch -vv                     # show each branch's tracked upstream + ahead/behind
git status                         # also reports ahead/behind vs. upstream
```

## Forks and multiple remotes

Contributing to a project you don’t have push access to usually means
forking it on the host, then adding both your fork and the original as
remotes so you can pull in upstream changes:

```bash
git remote add origin git@github.com:you/repo.git
git remote add upstream git@github.com:original-owner/repo.git
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main       # or: git rebase upstream/main
```

Next: [Undoing Changes](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/undoing-changes/) covers safely
walking back mistakes, both local and already-pushed.

## Renaming, removing, and mirroring remotes

```bash
git remote rename origin upstream       # rename a remote
git remote remove upstream              # remove a remote entirely
git remote set-url origin <new-url>     # switch a remote's URL (e.g. HTTPS → SSH)
git remote -v                           # list remotes with their fetch/push URLs
```

It’s common to have both an `origin` (your fork, which you push
to) and an `upstream` (the original project, which you only fetch
from) when contributing to someone else’s repository:

```bash
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original/repo.git
git fetch upstream
git rebase upstream/main   # replay your work on top of the latest upstream
```
Everyday Git.Undoing Changes:
Which command you want depends entirely on *where* the change you want to
undo currently lives: working directory, staging area, or already
committed (and possibly already pushed).

## Quick decision guide

| You want to… | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Discard unstaged edits to a file | `git restore <file>` |
| Unstage a file (keep the edits) | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| Rewrite the last commit's message/content | `git commit --amend` |
| Move the branch pointer, keep changes in the working dir | `git reset --mixed <commit>` (default) |
| Move the branch pointer and discard all changes | `git reset --hard <commit>` |
| Undo an already-pushed commit safely | `git revert <commit>` |
| Recover a commit you think you lost | `git reflog` |

## Working directory & staging area: git restore

```bash
git restore file.txt              # discard unstaged changes to a file
git restore .                     # discard all unstaged changes
git restore --staged file.txt     # unstage, keep the edits in place
git restore --source=HEAD~1 file.txt   # revert a file to an older commit's version
```

## Moving the branch pointer: git reset

`git reset <commit>` moves the current branch to point at `<commit>`. What
happens to everything after that point depends on the flag:

| Mode | Branch pointer | Staging area | Working directory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--soft` | moved | unchanged (still has the undone commits' changes staged) | unchanged |
| `--mixed` (default) | moved | reset to match target | unchanged (changes become unstaged) |
| `--hard` | moved | reset to match target | reset to match target — **destructive** |

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1     # undo last commit, keep changes staged
git reset HEAD~1            # undo last commit, keep changes unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1     # undo last commit and discard the changes entirely
git reset --hard origin/main # throw away local commits, match the remote exactly
```

> `--hard` permanently discards uncommitted work in the reset range. Double
> check `git status` and `git diff` before running it. Never `reset` commits
> that have already been pushed and might be in someone else’s history — use
> `revert` instead.

## Undoing a public commit: git revert

`git revert` creates a *new* commit that applies the inverse of an existing
one, leaving history intact — safe for commits others may have already
pulled:

```bash
git revert <sha>             # revert one commit
git revert HEAD~3..HEAD      # revert a range
git revert --no-commit <sha> # stage the revert without committing yet
```

## Recovering lost commits: the reflog

Git rarely deletes a commit outright — even after a `reset --hard` or a
branch deletion, the commit objects usually stick around until garbage
collected. The **reflog** records every position `HEAD` has pointed to:

```bash
git reflog                       # list recent HEAD movements with their SHAs
git checkout <sha-from-reflog>   # inspect a "lost" commit
git branch recovered <sha>       # turn it back into a real branch
```

The reflog is local-only (not pushed or cloned) and entries expire after
90 days by default (`gc.reflogExpire`) — treat it as a safety net, not
permanent storage.

## Removing untracked files

```bash
git clean -n     # dry run: show what would be deleted
git clean -f     # delete untracked files
git clean -fd    # also delete untracked directories
```

## Choosing the right tool

| Situation | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Unstaged edit you want to discard | `git restore <file>` |
| Staged change you want to unstage (keep the edit) | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| Local commits not yet pushed, want them gone | `git reset --hard HEAD~N` |
| Local commits not yet pushed, want to keep the edits unstaged | `git reset HEAD~N` |
| Already-pushed commit, shared history | `git revert <sha>` |
| “I reset --hard and now I need it back” | `git reflog` + `git reset --hard <sha>` |

The rule of thumb: **reset rewrites history** (fine locally, dangerous
once pushed and pulled by others), while **revert adds a new commit**
that undoes an old one (safe on shared branches, preserves the record that
something happened and was later undone).

## A worked example: the three reset modes, side by side

Starting point — `config.txt` contains `debug=false`, and
you've just committed a change to `debug=true` plus staged (but not
committed) an unrelated edit to `readme.md`:

```
$ git log --oneline -2
91bce02 Enable debug mode        ← the commit you want to undo
3af92c1 Initial commit

$ cat config.txt
debug=true

$ git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
        modified:   readme.md
```

Running each reset mode from this exact state produces a different
result:

```
$ git reset --soft HEAD~1
$ git log --oneline -1
3af92c1 Initial commit
$ cat config.txt
debug=true                     ← unchanged: still on disk
$ git status
Changes to be committed:
        modified:   config.txt   ← the undone commit's change is now staged
        modified:   readme.md    ← your earlier staged edit, untouched
```

```
$ git reset HEAD~1              # --mixed, the default
$ cat config.txt
debug=true                     ← still unchanged on disk
$ git status
Changes not staged for commit:
        modified:   config.txt   ← same change, but now UNstaged
Changes to be committed:
        modified:   readme.md    ← unaffected either way
```

```
$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
$ cat config.txt
debug=false                    ← reverted on disk too — the edit is gone
$ git status
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

Only `--hard` touched the actual file content — `--soft` and
`--mixed` only ever move the branch pointer and the staging area,
never the working directory, which is why they're the safe ones to reach
for when you're not sure yet.
Everyday Git.Stashing:
`git stash` shelves uncommitted changes — both staged and unstaged — onto
a stack, resetting your working directory to match `HEAD`, so you can
switch tasks (e.g. to fix an urgent bug on another branch) without
committing unfinished work.

## Basic usage

```bash
git stash                        # stash tracked changes, staged + unstaged
git stash push -m "wip: parser"  # stash with a descriptive message
git stash list                   # show the stash stack
git stash pop                    # reapply the most recent stash and remove it
git stash apply                  # reapply the most recent stash, keep it in the list
git stash drop                   # delete the most recent stash without applying it
git stash clear                  # delete every stash
```

## Working with a specific stash

The stack is indexed `stash@{0}` (newest) upward:

```bash
git stash show stash@{1}         # show summary of a specific stash
git stash show -p stash@{1}      # show its full diff
git stash apply stash@{1}        # apply a specific (non-latest) stash
git stash drop stash@{1}         # drop a specific stash
```

## Useful options

```bash
git stash -u          # also stash untracked files
git stash -a          # also stash ignored files
git stash push -- path/to/file    # stash changes to one path only
git stash branch new-branch       # create a branch from a stash and apply it there
```

`git stash branch` is the safe option when applying a stash would conflict
with how the current branch has moved on — it checks out a new branch from
the commit the stash was originally based on, then applies the stash there.

> A stash is stored as regular Git commits (under `refs/stash`), not magic
> — which is also why it survives things like `git gc` less reliably than a
> real branch. Don’t treat the stash as long-term storage for work you care
> about; commit to a branch instead if you’ll need it more than a day or two.

## Workflow tips

Stashes are a stack, so `git stash pop` always applies the most
recent one. If you have several in flight and need a specific one, list them
first and use the index shown:

```bash
git stash list
# stash@{0}: WIP on main: 3af92c1 add search bar
# stash@{1}: WIP on main: 91bce02 fix pagination

git stash show -p stash@{1}   # preview a specific stash's full diff before applying
```

A stash isn’t reachable from any branch, which means it *can* be
garbage-collected in rare cases (e.g. after `git gc --aggressive` on
a very old, un-referenced stash). Don’t treat the stash as long-term
storage — for work you want to keep around for more than a day or two,
commit it to a throwaway branch instead.

## A worked example: an urgent interruption

You're mid-way through a feature, three files deep in half-finished
changes, when a teammate reports a bug on `main`:

```
$ git status
On branch feature/search
Changes not staged for commit:
        modified:   search.js
        modified:   search.css
Untracked files:
        search-icon.svg
```

You can't commit this — it doesn't even run yet. Stash it instead:

```
$ git stash push -u -m "wip: search feature, icon not wired up yet"
Saved working directory and index state On feature/search: wip: search feature, icon not wired up yet

$ git status
On branch feature/search
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

`-u` included the untracked `search-icon.svg` too — without it,
a plain `git stash` would have left that file sitting on disk
(untracked files aren't stashed by default), which would then confusingly
follow you onto `main`.

```
$ git switch main
$ # ...fix the bug, commit, push...
$ git switch feature/search
$ git stash pop
On branch feature/search
Changes not staged for commit:
        modified:   search.js
        modified:   search.css
Untracked files:
        search-icon.svg
Dropped refs/stash@{0}
```

Exactly the state you left, restored in full — as if the interruption
never happened.
Everyday Git.Tags:
A tag is a ref that, unlike a branch, doesn’t move — it permanently marks
one specific commit, most commonly used for release versions
(`v1.0.0`, `v2.3.1`).

## Lightweight vs. annotated

|  | Lightweight | Annotated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A plain pointer to a commit | A full object: tagger, date, message, optional GPG signature |
| Create with | `git tag v1.0.0` | `git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0"` |
| Use for | Private, throwaway bookmarks | Public releases — almost always the right choice |

## Creating tags

```bash
git tag v1.0.0                              # lightweight, on HEAD
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0"         # annotated, on HEAD
git tag -a v0.9.0 <sha> -m "Retroactive tag" # annotated, on a specific commit
git tag -s v1.0.0 -m "Release 1.0.0"         # GPG-signed annotated tag
```

## Listing and inspecting

```bash
git tag                          # list all tags
git tag -l "v1.*"                # filter by pattern
git show v1.0.0                  # show the tag's message and the commit it points to
```

## Pushing tags

Tags are **not** pushed by a plain `git push` — they need to be pushed
explicitly:

```bash
git push origin v1.0.0        # push one tag
git push origin --tags        # push every local tag
git push --follow-tags        # push commits + any annotated tags reachable from them
```

## Checking out a tag

```bash
git checkout v1.0.0            # detached HEAD at that commit
git switch -c hotfix v1.0.0    # branch off a tag instead, if you'll commit
```

## Deleting tags

```bash
git tag -d v1.0.0                    # delete locally
git push origin --delete v1.0.0      # delete on the remote
```

## Signed tags

For release tags in particular, a GPG-signed annotated tag lets anyone
verify the tag really came from you and hasn’t been tampered with:

```bash
git tag -s v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"   # sign with your default GPG key
git tag -v v1.4.0                      # verify a signed tag's signature
git config --global user.signingkey <KEYID>  # set which key to use
git config --global tag.gpgSign true   # sign every annotated tag automatically
```

GitHub, GitLab, and similar hosts show a “Verified” badge next to
signed tags and commits when the signing key has been added to your
account, which is the main practical benefit for most projects.

Learn by Examples.Starting the Project:
This section is different from the rest of the docs: instead of one command
per page, we follow a **single real project from day one to first release**,
across several pages, and use a normal day's worth of Git commands at each
step — exactly in the order you'd actually reach for them. If [A Complete
Walkthrough](/git/0.0.0/getting-started/a-complete-walkthrough/) taught you what `git init` and
`git commit` actually do, this section is the next level up: a whole
project's worth of branches, conflicts, mistakes, stashes, releases, and
collaboration, back to back.

The project is `wordcount`, a tiny Dart command-line tool that counts words
in a text file. It's small enough to read in full, but real enough to need
every command in this section. The user throughout is `psdk`, working on
Arch Linux.

By the end of this section you will have:

- Initialized a project and made a clean history of small commits
- Built a feature on its own branch and merged it
- Caused and resolved a real merge conflict
- Undone a bad commit, a bad `add`, and a bad merge
- Stashed work to context-switch, and come back to it
- Rewritten local history with an interactive rebase before sharing it
- Tagged and shipped a release
- Pushed to a remote, opened a pull request, and reviewed one
- Shipped an emergency hotfix without disturbing unfinished work

Each page continues exactly where the last one left off — the same
repository, growing commit by commit — so if you skip ahead, `git log`
won't match what's shown. Follow it top to bottom the first time through.

## 1. Setting up

Assumes Git is already installed and configured — see
[Getting Started](/git/0.0.0/getting-started/getting-started/) if not.

```
$ mkdir wordcount && cd wordcount
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/psdk/wordcount/.git/
```

Since this is a Dart project, ignore Dart's build output and tool state
from the very first commit, before anything gets a chance to be tracked
by accident:

```
$ cat > .gitignore << 'EOF'
.dart_tool/
.packages
build/
*.exe
EOF
```

A `.gitignore` written *before* your first `dart pub get` means Git never
even offers to track generated files — much less annoying than untracking
them later. See [Configuration](/git/0.0.0/reference/configuration/) for more on
`.gitignore` patterns and a global ignore file for editor/OS cruft.

## 2. The first commit

```
$ cat > pubspec.yaml << 'EOF'
name: wordcount
description: Count words in a text file.
version: 0.1.0
environment:
  sdk: ^3.4.0
EOF

$ mkdir bin
$ cat > bin/wordcount.dart << 'EOF'
void main(List<String> args) {
  print('wordcount: no arguments yet');
}
EOF
```

```
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        .gitignore
        bin/wordcount.dart
        pubspec.yaml

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
```

Stage everything and make the first commit:

```
$ git add .
$ git commit -m "Initial commit: project skeleton"
[main (root-commit) 8f1a2c3] Initial commit: project skeleton
 3 files changed, 12 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 create mode 100644 bin/wordcount.dart
 create mode 100644 pubspec.yaml
```

`git add .` from the repository root stages every new and modified file
that isn't ignored — fine for a first commit like this one where
everything really does belong together. Once a project is underway,
prefer staging deliberately (`git add <file>` or `git add -p`, covered on
[Basic Workflow](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/basic-workflow/)) so unrelated changes don't end up in the
same commit by accident.

## 3. A second, focused commit

Real projects don't stop at a skeleton. Add the actual counting logic as
its own commit, separate from the scaffolding:

```
$ cat > bin/wordcount.dart << 'EOF'
import 'dart:io';

int countWords(String text) {
  final trimmed = text.trim();
  if (trimmed.isEmpty) return 0;
  return trimmed.split(RegExp(r'\s+')).length;
}

void main(List<String> args) {
  if (args.isEmpty) {
    stderr.writeln('usage: wordcount <file>');
    exit(64);
  }
  final text = File(args.first).readAsStringSync();
  print(countWords(text));
}
EOF
```

```
$ git add bin/wordcount.dart
$ git commit -m "Implement word counting"
[main 4b7e991] Implement word counting
 1 file changed, 13 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
```

```
$ git log --oneline
4b7e991 Implement word counting
8f1a2c3 Initial commit: project skeleton
```

Two commits in, and already a pattern worth keeping for the rest of the
project: **one logical change per commit**, with a message describing
*what* changed and, when it's not obvious, *why*. This is what makes
`git log`, `git blame`, and `git bisect` (see
[Bisecting](/git/0.0.0/advanced/bisecting/)) actually useful months from now instead of
a wall of "fix stuff" messages.

Continue to [Branching for a Feature](/git/0.0.0/learn-by-examples/branching-for-a-feature/),
where `wordcount` grows a second command-line flag on its own branch.
Learn by Examples.Fixing Mistakes:
Continuing from [Merging and a Real Conflict](/git/0.0.0/learn-by-examples/merging-and-a-real-conflict/).
Every real project accumulates small mistakes. This page walks through
three of the most common ones on `wordcount`, using the tool that
actually fits each — see [Undoing Changes](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/undoing-changes/) for
the full decision tree this page is drawing from.

## 1. "I staged a file I didn't mean to"

Add a debug script while poking at a bug, then stage everything without
looking closely:

```
$ cat > debug.dart << 'EOF'
void main() => print('temporary debug script, do not commit');
EOF
$ git add .
$ git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        new file:   debug.dart
```

Caught before committing — unstage it without touching the file itself:

```
$ git restore --staged debug.dart
$ git status
On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        debug.dart
```

`debug.dart` still exists on disk, still says what it says — only its
*staged* status changed. Since it should never be committed at all,
delete it and add it to `.gitignore` so it can't happen again:

```
$ rm debug.dart
$ echo 'debug.dart' >> .gitignore
$ git add .gitignore
$ git commit -m "Ignore local debug script"
[main a1b2c3d] Ignore local debug script
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

## 2. "I already committed, and the message is wrong"

```
$ cat >> bin/wordcount.dart << 'EOF'
// TODO: handle missing file gracefully
EOF
$ git add bin/wordcount.dart
$ git commit -m "wip"
[main f4e5d6c] wip
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

`"wip"` is not a message anyone will thank you for in six months. As
long as this commit **hasn't been pushed**, rewrite it in place:

```
$ git commit --amend -m "Note missing-file handling as a TODO"
[main 8d7c6b5] Note missing-file handling as a TODO
 Date: Thu Sep 4 09:12:03 2026 +0200
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

```
$ git log --oneline -1
8d7c6b5 Note missing-file handling as a TODO
```

`--amend` didn't add a new commit — it replaced the last one with a new
commit that has a new SHA. That's the rule to remember: `--amend`
**rewrites history**, so only use it on commits nobody else has already
pulled. If you'd also changed files before running it (`git add` first),
those changes would have been folded into the amended commit too, not
just the message.

## 3. "I need to undo the last commit entirely"

Say the TODO commit above turns out to be pointless noise and shouldn't
exist at all, not even reworded:

```
$ git log --oneline -3
8d7c6b5 Note missing-file handling as a TODO
a1b2c3d Ignore local debug script
9c3b7a2 Merge branch 'feature/help-flag'
```

```
$ git reset --soft HEAD~1
$ git log --oneline -3
a1b2c3d Ignore local debug script
9c3b7a2 Merge branch 'feature/help-flag'
7aa10f4 Add --words-only flag
$ git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        modified:   bin/wordcount.dart
```

`--soft` moved the branch pointer back one commit but left the change
staged — useful when you want to redo the commit differently. To throw
the change away entirely instead, `--hard` would have deleted it from
the working directory too. Here, discard it on purpose:

```
$ git restore --staged bin/wordcount.dart
$ git restore bin/wordcount.dart
$ git status
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

## 4. "I merged the wrong branch"

Simulate merging an abandoned experiment by accident:

```
$ git switch -c experiment/broken-idea
Switched to a new branch 'experiment/broken-idea'
$ echo 'this should never have shipped' > mistake.txt
$ git add mistake.txt
$ git commit -m "Experimental idea"
[experiment/broken-idea 2f1e0d9] Experimental idea
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

$ git switch main
$ git merge experiment/broken-idea
Updating a1b2c3d..2f1e0d9
Fast-forward
 mistake.txt | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

Caught immediately, before pushing — `git reflog` shows exactly where
`main` was a moment ago:

```
$ git reflog -5
2f1e0d9 (HEAD -> main) HEAD@{0}: merge experiment/broken-idea: Fast-forward
a1b2c3d HEAD@{1}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
8d7c6b5 HEAD@{2}: commit: Note missing-file handling as a TODO
a1b2c3d HEAD@{3}: commit: Ignore local debug script
9c3b7a2 HEAD@{4}: checkout: main
```

```
$ git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
HEAD is now at a1b2c3d Ignore local debug script
```

`main` is back to exactly where it was before the bad merge, and
`mistake.txt` is gone from the working directory too, because this reset
was `--hard`. The reflog is local-only and expires eventually, but for a
mistake caught the same day, it's the closest thing Git has to an undo
button for *anything* — including resets themselves.

```
$ git branch -D experiment/broken-idea
Deleted branch experiment/broken-idea (was 2f1e0d9).
```

`-D` (capital) force-deletes a branch even though its commit was never
merged into anything else — appropriate here specifically because the
branch was a dead end. `-d` (lowercase) would have refused, as a safety
check, precisely to catch this situation when it's *not* intentional.

## 5. "This was already pushed — I can't rewrite it"

Everything above rewrote history that only existed locally. Once a
commit is on a shared remote and someone else may have pulled it,
rewriting it out from under them causes real pain on their end. The safe
tool for a pushed mistake is `git revert`, which adds a *new* commit that
undoes the old one, leaving history intact:

```
$ git revert a1b2c3d --no-edit
[main 5e4d3c2] Revert "Ignore local debug script"
 1 file changed, 1 deletion(-)
```

Both commits are now visible in the log — the original and its
undo — which is exactly the point: anyone who already has the old commit
can pull this one without any conflict or confusion.

## 1. What the history actually looks like

```
$ git log --oneline main..feature/stdin-support
c4d5e6f Read from stdin when no file argument is given
d5e6f7a fix typo
e6f7a8b Read from stdin when no file argument is given
```

Three commits, but really only one idea — the middle two are just the
process of getting there. (This happens naturally: you commit, notice a
typo, commit the fix, and never bother cleaning it up until now.)

## 2. Starting the interactive rebase

```
$ git rebase -i main
```

Git opens an editor with one line per commit, oldest first:

```
pick e6f7a8b Read from stdin when no file argument is given
pick d5e6f7a fix typo
pick c4d5e6f Read from stdin when no file argument is given

# Rebase b3c4d5e..c4d5e6f onto b3c4d5e (3 commands)
#
# Commands:
# p, pick <commit> = use commit
# r, reword <commit> = use commit, but edit the commit message
# s, squash <commit> = use commit, but meld into previous commit
# f, fixup <commit> = like "squash", but discard this commit's log message
# d, drop <commit> = remove commit
```

This is a to-do list, not a log — editing it and saving tells Git how to
replay these three commits on top of `main`. Change it to squash the
typo-fix into the commit before it, and reword the final result:

```
pick e6f7a8b Read from stdin when no file argument is given
fixup d5e6f7a fix typo
reword c4d5e6f Read from stdin when no file argument is given
```

`fixup` folds a commit into the one above it and throws away its message
entirely (use `squash` instead if you wanted to keep and edit both
messages together). Save and close the editor.

## 3. Following through on each stop

Because line 3 is `reword`, Git pauses there and opens the editor again
with that commit's message, ready to edit:

```
Read from stdin when no file argument is given

# Please enter the commit message for your changes.
```

Change it to describe the finished feature as a whole:

```
Add stdin support for input with no file argument
```

Save and close. Git finishes replaying the commits:

```
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/stdin-support.
```

```
$ git log --oneline main..feature/stdin-support
a7b8c9d Add stdin support for input with no file argument
```

Three commits became one, with a message describing the feature rather
than the journey to it. The SHAs for every commit on this branch changed
in the process — this is exactly why rebasing is safe here (nobody else
has these commits yet) and would *not* be safe on a branch someone else
had already pulled, per [Rebasing & Cherry-Picking](/git/0.0.0/advanced/rebasing-&-cherry-picking/).

## 4. When a rebase hits a conflict

Had `main` moved since this branch started — say, another hotfix
landed — the rebase could have paused mid-replay with a conflict, looking
almost identical to a merge conflict:

```
$ git rebase main
Auto-merging bin/wordcount.dart
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in bin/wordcount.dart
error: could not apply a7b8c9d... Add stdin support for input with no file argument
```

The resolution steps are the same as any conflict — edit the file,
remove the `<<<<<<<`/`=======`/`>>>>>>>` markers, decide what the correct
combined code is — but finish it with rebase's own commands instead of
`git commit`:

```
$ git add bin/wordcount.dart
$ git rebase --continue
```

If a rebase conflict turns out to be more trouble than it's worth
mid-way through, `git rebase --abort` puts the branch back exactly how
it was before the rebase started, no matter how many commits in you are.

```
$ git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "wordcount 1.0.0: word, line, char counts; stdin support"
```

`-a` makes this an **annotated** tag — a real object in Git's database
with its own message, tagger name, and date, and the kind
[Tags](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/tags/) recommends for anything you'd call a release.  A
plain `git tag v1.0.0` (no `-a`) creates a **lightweight** tag instead: a
bare pointer to the commit with none of that metadata, fine for a
personal bookmark but not what you want other people relying on.

```
$ git show v1.0.0
tag v1.0.0
Tagger: psdk <psdk@example.com>
Date:   Thu Sep 4 09:40:00 2026 +0200

wordcount 1.0.0: word, line, char counts; stdin support

commit 1a2b3c4...
Author: psdk <psdk@example.com>
Date:   Thu Sep 4 09:38:00 2026 +0200

    Bump version to 1.0.0
```

```
$ git tag
v1.0.0
```

## 3. Tags don't move, branches do

This distinction matters immediately once work continues:

```
$ echo "print('debug marker');" >> bin/wordcount.dart
$ git add bin/wordcount.dart
$ git commit -m "Temporary debug print (do not release)"
[main 2b3c4d5] Temporary debug print (do not release)
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
```

```
$ git log --oneline -2
2b3c4d5 Temporary debug print (do not release)
1a2b3c4 Bump version to 1.0.0
```

`main` now points at `2b3c4d5`, one commit ahead of the tag. `v1.0.0`
still points at `1a2b3c4` — exactly the commit it was created on — and
always will, unless someone deliberately force-moves it. Check out the
tag directly to see this:

```
$ git checkout v1.0.0
Note: switching to 'v1.0.0'.

You are in 'detached HEAD' state...

HEAD is now at 1a2b3c4 Bump version to 1.0.0
```

This is the "detached HEAD" state covered in the
[FAQ](/git/0.0.0/reference/faq/) — `HEAD` points straight at the tagged commit rather
than at a branch. It's the correct, expected way to look at exactly what
was released, and it's read-only in spirit: build and test here freely,
but don't commit unless you first run `git switch -c` to give any new
work a branch to live on.

```
$ git switch main
Previous HEAD position was 1a2b3c4 Bump version to 1.0.0
Switched to branch 'main'
```

Remove the debug print before it ships in anything real:

```
$ git revert HEAD --no-edit
[main 3c4d5e6] Revert "Temporary debug print (do not release)"

```

## 1. Connecting a remote

After creating an empty repository named `wordcount` on GitHub (no

```
origin  git@github.com:psdk/wordcount.git (fetch)
origin  git@github.com:psdk/wordcount.git (push)
```

`origin` is just a conventional name for "the main remote" — Git doesn't
treat it specially, but nearly every tool and tutorial assumes it, so
there's rarely a reason to call it anything else. This example uses SSH;
see [Getting Started](/git/0.0.0/getting-started/getting-started/) for setting up an SSH key
or an HTTPS token if that step hasn't happened yet.

Add a `README.md` on its own branch rather than committing straight to

```
$ git switch -c docs/readme
Switched to a new branch 'docs/readme'
$ cat > README.md << 'EOF'

A tiny command-line word, line, and character counter, written in Dart.

## Usage

    dart run bin/wordcount.dart [--words-only] <file>
```

## 4. Reviewing someone else's pull request locally

A collaborator opens a pull request from `feature/csv-output`. To
actually run their code rather than just reading the diff on GitHub:

```
$ git fetch origin
remote: Enumerating objects: 6, done.
...
From github.com:psdk/wordcount
 * [new branch]      feature/csv-output -> origin/feature/csv-output
```

`fetch` downloads the new commits and updates `origin/feature/csv-output`,
a **remote-tracking branch** — but doesn't touch anything in the working
directory, unlike `pull`. See [Remotes](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/remotes/) for exactly what
distinguishes `fetch` from `pull` (spoiler: `pull` is `fetch` followed
by a `merge`, automatically).

```
$ git switch feature/csv-output
branch 'feature/csv-output' set up to track 'origin/feature/csv-output'.
Switched to a new branch 'feature/csv-output'
```

```
$ dart run bin/wordcount.dart --csv sample.txt

2,3,18
```

Looks correct. Leave review comments on GitHub, or make a small fixup
commit directly and push it back to the same branch — either is normal:

```
$ cat >> README.md << 'EOF'

Add `--csv` for comma-separated output.
EOF
$ git add README.md
$ git commit -m "Document --csv flag"
[feature/csv-output 5e6f7a8] Document --csv flag
$ git push
To github.com:psdk/wordcount.git

```

Because this branch already tracks `origin/feature/csv-output` (fetch
and switch set that up automatically), a plain `git push` with no
arguments knows exactly where to send it.

## 5. Keeping a branch up to date with main

While that pull request sits open, `main` moves on. Before it's merged,
bring it up to date so the merge on GitHub stays a clean fast-forward
where possible:

```
$ git switch feature/csv-output
$ git fetch origin
$ git rebase origin/main
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/csv-output.
$ git push --force-with-lease
```

`--force-with-lease` is required here because rebasing rewrote this
branch's commits (new SHAs, same as in
[Cleaning Up History Before Sharing](/git/0.0.0/learn-by-examples/cleaning-up-history-before-sharing/)),
so the remote's version and the local version no longer share a history
a plain push could reconcile. `--force-with-lease` (rather than plain
`--force`) refuses the push if anyone else has pushed to this branch
since your last fetch — protecting a collaborator's work from being
silently overwritten, which a bare `--force` would not do.

## The situation

It's later in the week. Locally, `feature/json-output` is half-written
and doesn't compile. Then a user reports that `v1.0.0` crashes on empty
input in a way that made it past review. It needs a fix, released, today
— without losing the half-finished feature.

## 1. Set aside the unfinished work

```
$ git status
On branch feature/json-output
Changes not staged for commit:
        modified:   bin/wordcount.dart
```

```
$ git stash push -m "WIP: JSON output, does not compile yet"
Saved working directory and index state On feature/json-output: \
  5e6f7a8 WIP: JSON output, does not compile yet
```

Same move as
[Stashing to Switch Context](/git/0.0.0/learn-by-examples/stashing-to-switch-context/):
the working directory is clean, and nothing is lost.

## 2. Reproduce the bug against the release, exactly

```
$ git switch main
$ git fetch origin
$ git switch -c hotfix/empty-stdin-crash v1.0.0
Switched to a new branch 'hotfix/empty-stdin-crash'
```

Branching from the **tag**, not from `main`, matters here: `main` may
already contain unrelated in-progress changes since `v1.0.0` shipped, and
the hotfix needs to be exactly `v1.0.0` plus the fix — nothing more —
so it can be verified against precisely what users actually have.

```
$ echo -n "" | dart run bin/wordcount.dart
Unhandled exception:
RangeError (index): Invalid value: Valid value range is empty: 0
```

Confirmed — reproduced on the exact released code.

## What just happened, end to end

In one afternoon, without losing any work or touching anyone else's:

- Unfinished, non-compiling work was set aside with **stash**
- A **tag** provided an exact, reproducible target for the bug
- A **branch off the tag** isolated the fix from unrelated in-progress
  work on `main`
- The fix was **committed**, **tagged** as a patch release, and **merged**
  back into `main`, handling the fast-forward-or-merge-commit question
  either way it came out
- Both the branch and the tag were **pushed**
- The feature branch **merged in the fix** from `main`, and the stash was
  **popped** back on top of it
