Productivity.Aliases & Shortcuts:
Git lets you define custom subcommands — both simple word
substitutions and full shell one-liners — so the commands you run
fifty times a day can be three letters instead of fifteen.

## Basic aliases

Anything after `alias.` becomes runnable as `git <name>`:

```bash
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.ci commit
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.unstage "restore --staged"
```

These write directly into `~/.gitconfig`, so you can also edit the
`[alias]` section by hand:

```toml
[alias]
    co = checkout
    br = branch
    ci = commit
    st = status
    unstage = restore --staged
```

## A useful starter set

```toml
[alias]
    lg = log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
    last = log -1 HEAD --stat
    amend = commit --amend --no-edit
    undo = reset --soft HEAD~1
    aliases = config --get-regexp alias
```

`git aliases` (once defined) lists every alias you have configured
— handy after a few years of accumulating them across machines.

## Aliases that run shell commands

Prefix the value with `!` to run it through the shell instead of as
a Git subcommand. This unlocks pipelines, multiple commands, and anything
else a shell can do:

```toml
[alias]
    root = !pwd
    save  = !git add -A && git commit -m "WIP"
    graph = !git log --graph --pretty=format:'%C(auto)%h%d %s %C(black)%C(bold)%cr' --all
    cleanup = !git branch --merged main | grep -v 'main$' | xargs -r git branch -d
```

Shell aliases run from the repository root by default (Git sets
`GIT_PREFIX` and changes directory for you), and receive any extra
arguments you pass after the alias name via `"$@"`:

```toml
[alias]
    who = !"f() { git log --author=\"$1\" --oneline; }; f"
```

Called as `git who "Jane Doe"`.

## Beyond aliases: shell functions

For anything that needs to run *before* Git is even involved (like
creating a directory and cloning into it), a plain shell function in your
`.bashrc`/`.zshrc` is often simpler than a Git alias:

```
gclone() { git clone "$1" && cd "$(basename "$1" .git)"; }
```

> Aliases are per-machine unless you sync your dotfiles. If you use several
> machines, keeping `~/.gitconfig`'s `[alias]` section in a dotfiles
> repo (symlinked in) means new machines inherit your whole shortcut set
> immediately.
Productivity.Worktrees:
A **worktree** is a separate working directory, backed by the same
`.git` repository, checked out to a different branch (or the same
branch's different commit). It replaces the old habit of keeping several
full clones around, or stashing constantly to switch context.

## Why not just switch branches?

`git switch` changes what’s on disk in your *one* working
directory. If you're mid-way through a feature with a dirty working tree
and a P1 bug comes in, you'd normally have to stash, switch, fix, switch
back, and pop — worktrees let you keep both states on disk
simultaneously, each in its own directory, sharing one object database and
one set of remotes.

## Creating a worktree

```
# new worktree at ../hotfix, checking out an existing branch
git worktree add ../hotfix fix/123

# new worktree AND new branch in one step
git worktree add -b fix/456 ../fix-456 main
```

Each worktree behaves like a normal working directory — `cd` into
it and run any Git command as usual. Commits made there are immediately
visible from the main worktree's `git log --all`, since it's the same
underlying repository.

## Listing and removing worktrees

```bash
git worktree list                 # show every worktree and its branch/commit
git worktree remove ../hotfix      # clean removal (must be clean, no uncommitted changes)
git worktree prune                 # forget worktrees whose directories were deleted manually
```

A branch can only be checked out in *one* worktree at a time — Git
refuses to check out `main` in a second worktree while it's already
active in the first, to avoid two working directories silently diverging
on what should be the same branch.

## Common use cases

| Scenario | Why a worktree helps |
| --- | --- |
| Urgent hotfix while mid-feature | No stash/switch dance; both states stay on disk |
| Running a long test suite on `main` | Keep working in another worktree while it runs |
| Reviewing a PR locally | `git worktree add ../review pr-branch`, open in an editor, delete when done |
| Building release artifacts from a tag | Isolated checkout that won't disturb your active work |

## Caveats

- Submodules need `git submodule update --init` run separately in
  each worktree — they aren’t automatically initialized.
- Worktrees share the same `.git/config`, so repo-level (not global)
  config, hooks, and `.gitignore` apply identically everywhere.
- Deleting a worktree's directory with `rm -rf` instead of
  `git worktree remove` leaves stale metadata behind until you run
  `git worktree prune`.

Advanced.Rebasing & Cherry-Picking:
Where `merge` combines two histories with a new merge commit,
**rebase** rewrites one branch’s commits so they appear to start from a
different base — producing a linear history with no merge commits.

## Basic rebase

```bash
git switch feature-x
git rebase main
```

This takes every commit unique to `feature-x`, temporarily sets it aside,
resets `feature-x` to the tip of `main`, then replays each commit on top
one at a time — giving each a new SHA, since its parent changed.

## Merge vs. rebase

|  | Merge | Rebase |
| --- | --- | --- |
| History shape | Preserves exactly what happened, including a merge commit | Linear, as if the branch was written on top of the latest main |
| Original commit SHAs | Unchanged | Rewritten (new SHAs) |
| Safe on shared/pushed branches? | Yes, always | No — only rebase commits nobody else has pulled |
| Good for | Preserving true history, feature branches merged via PR | Cleaning up a local branch before opening a PR |

> **The golden rule of rebasing:** never rebase commits that exist outside
> your local repository, i.e. that you’ve already pushed and others might
> have based work on. Rewriting shared history forces everyone else to
> reconcile diverging SHAs by hand.

## Resolving conflicts during a rebase

```
# Git pauses at the first conflicting commit
git status                 # see what's conflicted
# edit files, resolve markers
git add <file>
git rebase --continue       # apply the next commit
git rebase --skip           # or: drop this commit entirely
git rebase --abort          # or: bail out, back to pre-rebase state
```

## Interactive rebase

`git rebase -i` opens an editable list of commits, letting you reorder,
edit, squash, or drop them before they’re replayed — the standard way to
clean up a messy local branch before pushing:

```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~5     # interactively edit the last 5 commits
git rebase -i main       # interactively edit everything since branching from main
```

The editor shows one line per commit with an action keyword you can change:

| Action | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `pick` | keep the commit as-is (default) |
| `reword` | keep the commit, but edit its message |
| `edit` | pause after applying, so you can amend it |
| `squash` | combine into the previous commit, merging messages |
| `fixup` | combine into the previous commit, discarding this message |
| `drop` | remove the commit entirely |

Reordering lines reorders the commits. Save and close the editor to run
the rebase with those instructions.

## Cherry-picking

`git cherry-pick` applies one specific commit from anywhere in the
repository’s history onto your current branch — useful for porting a
single fix to a release branch without merging everything else:

```bash
git cherry-pick <sha>               # apply one commit here
git cherry-pick <sha1> <sha2>       # apply several, in order
git cherry-pick A..B                # apply a range (exclusive of A)
git cherry-pick --no-commit <sha>   # stage the change without committing
git cherry-pick --continue          # after resolving a conflict
git cherry-pick --abort             # bail out
```

## Autosquash workflow

Mark small fixups against an earlier commit as you make them, then let
rebase sort out the ordering automatically:

```bash
git commit --fixup <sha>                       # create a fixup! commit
git rebase -i --autosquash <sha>~1              # auto-arranges + marks it "fixup"
```

## Range rebases with --onto

Sometimes you need to move a range of commits, not everything since a
common ancestor — for example, extracting a feature branch that was
accidentally built on top of another unmerged feature branch:

```
# replay everything after <since> up to feature-b onto main,
# dropping whatever feature-b originally branched from
git rebase --onto main <since> feature-b
```

This is one of the more advanced rebase forms; reach for it when
`git rebase main` alone would replay commits you don’t actually
want (because your branch point wasn’t `main`).
Advanced.Submodules:
A submodule embeds one Git repository inside another as a subdirectory,
pinned to a specific commit — used to vendor a dependency while keeping
its own independent history and remote.

## Adding a submodule

```bash
git submodule add https://github.com/example/lib.git libs/lib
git commit -m "Add lib submodule"
```

This creates a `.gitmodules` file (tracked, describes the mapping) and a
gitlink entry in the parent repo’s tree pointing at the submodule’s current
commit — the parent repo never stores the submodule’s files, only which
commit it’s pinned to.

## Cloning a repo that has submodules

Plain `git clone` leaves submodule directories empty. Either clone with a
flag, or initialize afterward:

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules <url>
# already cloned without it?
git submodule update --init --recursive
```

## Updating a submodule

```bash
cd libs/lib
git fetch
git checkout <new-sha-or-branch>
cd ../..
git add libs/lib
git commit -m "Bump lib submodule"
```

Or, to update every submodule to the latest commit on the branch each one
tracks:

```bash
git submodule update --remote --merge
```

## Other useful commands

```bash
git submodule status                 # current SHA of each submodule
git submodule foreach 'git status'   # run a command in every submodule
git submodule deinit libs/lib        # remove the working copy, keep the config
git rm libs/lib                      # fully remove the submodule
```

## Common pitfalls

- **Forgetting `--recurse-submodules`** on clone leaves empty
  directories that look broken but aren’t — run
  `git submodule update --init --recursive`.
- **Detached HEAD inside the submodule** is the normal state after an
  update — the parent repo tracks a commit, not a branch. Commit new work
  inside a submodule on an actual branch, or it’s easy to lose.
- **Forgetting to commit the pointer bump** in the parent repo after
  updating a submodule means everyone else still checks out the old
  commit.

Alternatives worth knowing about if submodules feel too heavyweight:
`git subtree` (built in, copies history into the parent repo instead of
pinning a pointer) and language-level package managers (npm, pub, cargo)
for anything that’s actually published as a package rather than vendored
source.

## Alternatives worth knowing about

Submodules have a reputation for being fiddly, largely because they
require an explicit `update` step that’s easy to forget. Two
common alternatives, depending on what you actually need:

- **git subtree** — merges the external project’s history
  directly into a subdirectory of your repo. No separate clone step for
  collaborators, but pushing changes back upstream is more involved.
  `git subtree add --prefix=vendor/lib https://github.com/org/lib.git main --squash`
- **Package managers** — for anything published as a proper
  package (npm, pub, cargo, pip, …), a real dependency manager is
  almost always a better fit than vendoring source via submodule.

Submodules still make sense when you need an exact, pinned copy of
another team’s *source* (not a published package) inside your build,
with the ability to patch and rebuild it locally.
Advanced.Hooks:
Hooks are executable scripts Git runs automatically at specific points in
its workflow — before a commit, after a checkout, before a push, and so
on — used for linting, running tests, enforcing commit message formats,
or notifying other systems.

## Where they live

Every repository gets a `.git/hooks/` directory pre-populated with
`*.sample` files. Drop the `.sample` suffix and make the file executable
to enable a hook:

```bash
mv .git/hooks/pre-commit.sample .git/hooks/pre-commit
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
```

> `.git/` is never committed, so hooks placed there aren’t shared with
> collaborators automatically. Teams typically manage hooks with a tool like
> [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com), [Husky](https://typicode.github.io/husky/),
> or a checked-in script plus `core.hooksPath` (below) instead.

## Commonly used hooks

| Hook | Runs | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pre-commit` | before a commit message is even prompted for | linting, formatting checks, running fast unit tests |
| `commit-msg` | after the message is written, before the commit is created | enforcing a message format (e.g. Conventional Commits) |
| `post-commit` | after a commit completes | notifications, triggering local build watchers |
| `pre-push` | before `git push` sends objects | running the full test suite, blocking pushes to protected branches |
| `pre-rebase` | before a rebase starts | blocking rebases of already-published branches |
| `post-checkout` | after `switch`/`checkout` | reinstalling dependencies when they've changed |
| `post-merge` | after a successful merge/pull | same, after pulling in new commits |

## Example: a pre-commit hook

```
#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/pre-commit
dart format --set-exit-if-changed . || {
  echo "Formatting issues found. Run 'dart format .' and try again."
  exit 1
}
```

Returning a non-zero exit status aborts the commit; the hook can also
`echo` to stderr to explain why.

## Sharing hooks across a team

Point Git at a checked-in directory instead of `.git/hooks`:

```bash
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

Commit a `.githooks/` directory with executable scripts, and every clone
that runs this config line will use them — a lightweight alternative to a
full hook manager for small teams.

## Server-side hooks

Bare repositories (the kind Git hosts store) also support hooks that run
on the server: `pre-receive`, `update`, and `post-receive`, used to reject
pushes that don’t meet a policy or to trigger CI/deployment. GitHub and
GitLab expose equivalent functionality through branch protection rules and
CI webhooks rather than raw server-side hooks, since you don’t have shell
access to their servers.

## Exit codes, and using a hook manager

A hook script’s exit code is what determines whether Git proceeds:
**0 allows the action, non-zero aborts it** (for hooks that support
aborting, like `pre-commit` and `pre-push`; a few informational
hooks like `post-commit` can’t block anything since the action has
already happened).

Hand-written hooks aren’t committed to the repo by default (they live
in the untracked `.git/hooks/`), so most teams use a hook manager that
stores hook config in a tracked file and installs the real scripts for
everyone:

| Tool | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| pre-commit | Python-based, config in a tracked `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, huge plugin ecosystem |
| husky | JS-ecosystem standard, config lives in `package.json` / `.husky/` |
| lefthook | Single Go binary, language-agnostic, fast on large monorepos |

All three work by installing a thin script into `.git/hooks/` that
delegates to the tracked config, which is exactly what `core.hooksPath`
does more directly if you don’t need the extra features.
Advanced.Bisecting:
`git bisect` finds the exact commit that introduced a bug by binary
search: you tell Git one commit that was **good** and one that’s
**bad**, and it checks out commits one at a time for you to test,
narrowing the range in half each time.

## Why it's faster than it sounds

For a bug introduced somewhere in the last 1,000 commits, checking each
one individually could take 1,000 tests. Binary search needs at most
⌈log₂(1000)⌉ = 10. This is the entire value proposition of
`bisect`: it turns a linear search into a logarithmic one.

## Manual workflow

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current commit (e.g. HEAD) is broken
git bisect good v1.2.0         # this known-good tag/commit works

# Git checks out a commit halfway between them. Test it, then:
git bisect good                # this commit is fine, bug is later
# or
git bisect bad                 # this commit is broken, bug is earlier

# repeat until Git prints the first bad commit
git bisect reset               # when done: return to your original HEAD
```

At each step Git prints how many revisions remain and roughly how many
more steps are needed, so you always know how much further there is to go.

## Automating it with a test script

If the bug can be detected by a script (a failing test, a command that
exits non-zero), skip the manual testing entirely:

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v1.2.0
git bisect run npm test         # or ./run-tests.sh, make check, etc.
```

Git runs the given command at each step and interprets its exit code:
`0` means good, any nonzero code (except 125) means bad. This can walk
through dozens of commits fully unattended and report the exact culprit
commit in seconds to minutes, depending on how long the test takes.

## Skipping untestable commits

Sometimes a commit in range simply doesn't build, or isn't testable for
unrelated reasons. Mark it as unknown instead of good/bad and Git will pick
a different commit to try:

```bash
git bisect skip
```

## Quick reference

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `git bisect start` | Begin a bisect session |
| `git bisect bad [<rev>]` | Mark a commit (default: HEAD) as bad |
| `git bisect good <rev>` | Mark a commit as good |
| `git bisect skip` | Skip an untestable commit |
| `git bisect run <cmd>` | Automate the whole search with a test command |
| `git bisect log` | Print the session's history (shareable/replayable) |
| `git bisect reset` | End the session, return to the original branch/commit |
Advanced.Patches & Diffs:
Not every change needs a pull request — sometimes the simplest way to
share a change is a plain text patch file. Git's diff format is also worth
understanding on its own, since it's what `git diff`, code review
tools, and `git apply` all speak.

## Reading a unified diff

```dart
diff --git a/src/main.dart b/src/main.dart
index 3af92c1..91bce02 100644
--- a/src/main.dart
+++ b/src/main.dart
@@ -10,7 +10,7 @@ void main() {
   print('starting');
-  var x = 1;
+  var x = 2;
   print('done');
 }
```

The `@@ -10,7 +10,7 @@` line is a **hunk header**: it means
the shown hunk starts at line 10 in the old file (7 lines shown) and line
10 in the new file (7 lines shown). Lines starting with `-` were
removed, `+` were added, and unmarked lines are context.

## Generating patch files

```
# uncommitted working-tree changes as a patch
git diff > my-changes.patch

# one specific commit
git format-patch -1 <sha>

# every commit on a branch since it diverged from main, one file each
git format-patch main..feature-branch

# the same, but as one combined file
git format-patch main..feature-branch --stdout > feature.patch
```

`format-patch` produces email-ready output (commit message, author,
date included as headers) — it's designed for the `git send-email`
workflow still used by projects like the Linux kernel, but the files work
fine as plain patches too.

## Applying patches

```bash
git apply my-changes.patch          # apply to the working tree, no commit created
git apply --check my-changes.patch  # dry run: verify it would apply cleanly
git am feature.patch                # apply AND create a commit, preserving author/message
git am *.patch                      # apply a whole format-patch series in order
```

Use `apply` for a plain diff you just want merged into your working
tree; use `am` ("apply mailbox") for files produced by
`format-patch`, since it reconstructs the original commit(s) including
their metadata rather than leaving everything unstaged.

## Useful diff options

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--stat` | Summary of files changed and line counts, no content |
| `--word-diff` | Highlight changed words instead of whole lines |
| `-U<n>` | Show n lines of context instead of the default 3 |
| `--stat --summary` | Include file mode changes, renames, creations |
| `-M` | Detect renames (on by default in most commands now) |
| `--no-color` | Plain output, useful when piping to another tool |

> A patch file only encodes a diff and (for `format-patch`) commit
> metadata — it does not include binary blob history the way a bundle or
> proper clone does. For sharing entire branches with someone offline,
> `git bundle` is usually a better fit than a pile of patch files.
Advanced.Attributes:
A `.gitattributes` file lets you control how Git treats specific
paths — line endings, diffing, merging, and what gets included when
exporting an archive — based on glob patterns, the same syntax used by
`.gitignore`.

## Normalizing line endings

The most common reason to reach for `.gitattributes`: force
consistent line endings in the repository regardless of what any individual
contributor's `core.autocrlf` is set to.

```
# .gitattributes
* text=auto
*.sh text eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.png binary
```

`text=auto` lets Git guess whether a file is text and normalize its
line endings to LF in the repository, converting to the platform's native
ending on checkout only if `core.autocrlf` calls for it. Explicit
`eol=lf`/`eol=crlf` overrides that per pattern — useful for
shell scripts that must stay LF even when checked out on Windows.

## Custom diff and merge drivers

Binary or generated files often produce useless diffs by default. Tell
Git to treat a file type specially:

```
# .gitattributes
*.docx diff=word
package-lock.json -diff
*.ipynb merge=union
```

`-diff` disables diffing entirely for a path (shown as "Binary files
differ"). `diff=word` refers to a driver you define separately in
config:

```bash
git config diff.word.textconv "pandoc --to=plain"
```

which converts the file to plain text before diffing, so
`git diff` on a `.docx` shows readable prose instead of binary
noise.

## Controlling git archive output

```
# .gitattributes
.github export-ignore
tests export-ignore
CHANGELOG.md export-ignore
```

`export-ignore` excludes matching paths from `git archive` (and
from the tarballs GitHub/GitLab generate for releases), letting you keep
CI config and tests out of a distributed source tarball without removing
them from the repository itself.

## Language detection (GitHub Linguist)

GitHub's "Languages" bar on a repo page reads `.gitattributes` too:

```
vendor/* linguist-vendored
*.g.dart linguist-generated
docs/* linguist-documentation
```

This keeps generated or vendored code from skewing the language
statistics — useful for e.g. a Dart project with a large
`vendor/` directory of copied C sources.

## Quick reference

| Attribute | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `text` / `-text` | Force/disable line-ending normalization |
| `eol=lf` / `eol=crlf` | Force a specific line ending on checkout |
| `binary` | Shorthand for `-text -diff` |
| `diff=<driver>` | Use a named external diff driver |
| `merge=<driver>` | Use a named merge strategy for conflicts in this path |
| `export-ignore` | Exclude from `git archive` output |
| `linguist-generated` | Hide from GitHub's diffs/stats as generated code |

Reference.Configuration:
## Configuration levels

Git reads config from three (or four) increasingly specific levels, each
overriding the last:

| Level | Flag | File |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System | `--system` | `/etc/gitconfig` |
| Global (user) | `--global` | `~/.gitconfig` |
| Local (repository) | `--local` (default) | `.git/config` |
| Worktree | `--worktree` | `.git/config.worktree` (needs `extensions.worktreeConfig`) |

```bash
git config --list --show-origin     # see every setting and where it came from
git config user.email               # read one value (checks all levels)
git config --global --edit          # open ~/.gitconfig in $EDITOR
```

## Commonly changed settings

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "nano"
git config --global pull.rebase true         # pull always rebases instead of merging
git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true # first push of a branch auto-sets upstream
git config --global core.autocrlf input       # line-ending normalization (Linux/macOS)
git config --global color.ui auto
```

## Aliases

Shorten frequently-typed commands:

```bash
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all"
git config --global alias.last "log -1 HEAD"
```

Then `git st` works exactly like `git status`. These live under
`[alias]` in `~/.gitconfig` and can also be edited there directly.

## .gitignore

Patterns of files Git should never track, one per line, checked in at the
repository root (or any subdirectory, for scoped rules):

```
*.log            # wildcard by extension
/build/          # only the top-level build directory
node_modules/    # anywhere in the tree
!important.log   # negate a previous pattern
```

A personal, global ignore file (for editor swap files, OS cruft, etc.)
that applies across every repository on your machine:

```bash
git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global
```

## .gitattributes

Controls how Git treats specific paths — line endings, diff behavior,
merge strategy, and marking generated files:

```
*.sh text eol=lf
*.png binary
*.min.js linguist-generated
pubspec.lock merge=ours
```

## Credential helpers

Avoid retyping a personal access token on every HTTPS push:

```
# Linux, cache in memory for 15 minutes
git config --global credential.helper cache
```

## Per-directory identities with conditional includes

If you use a different email for work and personal projects, conditional
includes apply a different config automatically based on where the
repository lives on disk — no per-repo setup required:

```
# in ~/.gitconfig
[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]
    path = ~/.gitconfig-work

# in ~/.gitconfig-work
[user]
    email = you@company.com
```

Any repository cloned under `~/work/` will now use the work email
automatically, while everything else keeps using the identity set in the
main `[user]` block.

## What’s the difference between Git and GitHub?

**Git** is the version control software itself — it runs entirely on
your machine and has no concept of "GitHub." **GitHub** (and GitLab,
Bitbucket, Codeberg, etc.) is a hosting service built *around* Git: it
stores remote copies of Git repositories and adds features Git itself
doesn’t have, like pull requests, issue tracking, and CI. You can use Git
fully without ever touching GitHub.

## What does "detached HEAD" mean, and is it a problem?

It means `HEAD` points directly at a commit instead of at a branch —
which happens when you check out a specific commit, a tag, or a
remote-tracking branch directly. It’s not an error state; you can look
around, build, and test freely. The only thing to watch for: any new
commits you make while detached aren’t on any branch, so they become
unreachable (and eventually garbage-collected) the moment you check out
something else — unless you first run `git switch -c new-branch-name` to
give them a home. See [How Git Works](/git/0.0.0/how-git-works/objects-&-the-.git-directory/).

## I just made a mistake. How do I undo it?

Depends what you did — see the decision table on
[Undoing Changes](/git/0.0.0/everyday-git/undoing-changes/). As a rule of thumb: if you
haven’t pushed yet, almost anything is fixable with `reset`, `restore`, or
`rebase -i`. If you have pushed, prefer `revert` over rewriting history.
Deleted a branch by accident? `git reflog` almost certainly still has it.

## Why is Git bad at handling large binary files?

Git computes diffs and deltas assuming text-like content that compresses
well between versions. Large binaries (videos, datasets, compiled
assets) don’t diff well, so every version is stored close to full size,
bloating the repository forever — even if the file is later deleted, old
versions remain in history. Use
[Git LFS](https://git-lfs.com) (Large File Storage), which stores a
small pointer file in Git and the actual binary content in separate
storage, for anything like this.

## Should I merge or rebase?

Merge when combining a finished feature branch back into `main` (and
especially anything already pushed/shared) — it preserves exactly what
happened. Rebase when cleaning up your own local, not-yet-shared branch
before opening a pull request, or keeping a long-lived feature branch
up to date with `main` without a pile of merge commits. Full comparison on
[Rebasing & Cherry-Picking](/git/0.0.0/advanced/rebasing-&-cherry-picking/).

## Should I clone over SSH or HTTPS?

Either works. SSH (`git@github.com:user/repo.git`) authenticates with a key
pair and never prompts for credentials once set up — generally preferred
for regular contributors. HTTPS
(`https://github.com/user/repo.git`) works anywhere without SSH access
(e.g. some corporate networks that block port 22) and authenticates with a
personal access token, cached by a
[credential helper](/git/0.0.0/reference/configuration/) so you don’t retype it
constantly.

## Why do commits show both "Author" and "Committer"?

The **author** is whoever originally wrote the change; the
**committer** is whoever last applied it to the repository. These are
usually the same person, but diverge when a patch is emailed to a
maintainer who applies it (author: contributor, committer: maintainer),
or after a rebase, which updates the committer date/identity while
preserving the original author.

## Why doesn’t Git track empty directories?

Git tracks content (blobs) and the trees that reference them — an empty
directory has no content to point at, so there’s nothing for Git to
record. The common workaround is committing a placeholder file inside it,
conventionally named `.gitkeep` (not a Git feature, just a naming
convention).

## A few more common questions

**How do I clone just the last few commits of a huge repo?**  
`git clone --depth 1 <url>` for a shallow clone with only the latest
commit's history. Useful for CI checkouts that only need the current
source, not full history.

**Why do my line endings keep changing on Windows?**  
Set `core.autocrlf true` on Windows (converts LF→CRLF on checkout,
back on commit) and `input` on Linux/macOS if you collaborate with
Windows users. See [Attributes](/git/0.0.0/advanced/attributes/) for per-file
control via `.gitattributes`, which is the more robust fix for a team.

**What's the difference between git bisect and just reading the log?**  
Bisect is a binary search: for N suspect commits it needs roughly
log₂(N) tests instead of checking every commit one by one, which matters
a lot once a regression is dozens or hundreds of commits old. See
[Bisecting](/git/0.0.0/advanced/bisecting/).
